Space generously: hills run about 8 feet apart on all sides for full-size types (closer for icebox and bush kinds), because a full-size vine can run 8 to 12 feet and wants about 24 square feet to itself. Black plastic mulch is a real help in shorter or cooler-summer areas, warming the soil and speeding an early start. old: Cherry tomatoes are almost always indeterminate: they grow, flower, and fruit all season until frost kills them. No stopping needed, but they need strong staking or caging. Some compact varieties (Tumbling Tom, Patio Choice) are technically determinate.
new: Tomatillos are indeterminate: they keep flowering and fruiting until frost, which allows multiple harvests through the season. Unlike tomatoes, which have both determinate and indeterminate varieties, all tomatillo varieties are indeterminate. Plants grow 3 to 4 feet tall and wide with a bushy, sprawling habit, and stems root where they touch the ground. Stake, cage, or trellis each plant to keep fruit off the ground and improve air circulation. Tomatillos weigh less than tomato plants, so they are easier to support. Habit varies by variety: Rendidora grows upright, while Gigante, Tamayo, Toma Verde, and Gulliver Hybrid sprawl more.

old: If your plant grows tall and leafy but produces very little fruit, or pale, flavorless tomatillos, sun is probably the problem. Tomatilloes need at least 6 hours of direct sun per day; below that, the plant puts its energy into growing stems and leaves instead of fruit. What fruit does form tends to be bland because sugar development depends on sunlight. A secondary sign: shaded plants tend to stay wet longer and get more disease, because leaves don't dry out well in low light. If your spot gets 4-5 hours, you'll get some fruit, but manage expectations: fewer tomatillos, smaller, and less sweet than a full-sun plant.

Wet leaves get diseases more easily, so if you water with a sprinkler, do it in the morning so the leaves dry before night.

old: Tomatilloes are among the most light-demanding vegetables: photosynthesis is the energy source for both vegetative growth and fruit sugar development, and fruit quality is directly proportional to the plant's photosynthetic output. Below 6 hours of direct sun, the plant redirects what energy it has toward survival, stem elongation and leaf area, rather than reproduction. Fruit set drops sharply, and what fruit does form is typically thin-skinned, pale, and bland. A secondary effect is increased disease: shaded plants stay wetter longer after rain or irrigation, and poor airflow through dense, etiolated growth creates the humid microclimate that blight and leaf mold need to establish.

A bushy, leafy plant that is slow to bear may also point to excess nitrogen, which produces exactly that growth. Foliar disease is a separate risk: wet leaves are more disease-prone, rainy periods or humid, windless days can encourage foliar diseases, and early blight, anthracnose, late blight, and tobacco mosaic virus can all affect tomatillos.

old: You'll see the leaves turn black or dark brown and go limp, sometimes overnight after a cold night. Tomatilloes have no cold tolerance at all. Even without a hard freeze, temperatures below 50°F cause what's called chilling injury: the plant's cells start to break down, and young transplants are especially vulnerable because they haven't built up a protective waxy coating yet. It's tempting to think the plant just needs time to recover, but if it was hit by frost, it usually won't come back. For next time: wait until both your nighttime lows and your soil temperature are reliably above 60°F before transplanting.

old: Tomatilloes are warm-season crops with tropical origin and have no cold tolerance mechanism, unlike brassicas or root vegetables, they cannot harden or acclimate to cold. Chilling injury begins below 50°F and cell damage accelerates near freezing; a single frost event at the transplant stage usually kills the plant outright because young transplants have not yet developed the protective waxy cuticle layer that provides some buffer in established plants. Soil temperature is as important as air temperature: roots in cold soil (below 60°F) cannot take up water or nutrients efficiently even when air temperatures are acceptable, which causes transplant shock that looks like cold damage but persists for weeks after the weather improves.

old: UF/IFAS ties spacing to the humidity inside the canopy rather than to water on the leaf, and that distinction is the whole point: powdery mildew infects without free water on the surface, so keeping the foliage dry is not the lever it is on most leaf diseases. Published spacing for oregano runs from 10 inches up to 18 inches depending on which extension source you read, so take the wider end in a humid summer, and thin an established clump rather than letting it close over. Site matters for the same reason: shade is a favoring condition for this fungus, so an open position is doing real work and not just growing better oregano.
new: UF/IFAS recommends spacing plants 10 to 12 inches apart to improve air circulation and prevent the extra humidity that attracts pests and diseases. To prevent powdery mildew, UF/IFAS pairs good air circulation with avoiding overhead watering. Oregano generally resists disease but can occasionally get powdery mildew or root rot, especially in humid conditions.

old: Oregano is a durable perennial in the Rio Grande Valley's frost-free winters. Texas A&M AgriLife's herb-growing guidance for the state calls for full sun and well-drained soil, spaced about 10 to 12 inches apart, and notes it is a perennial that becomes woody after a few years and is best dug and replanted at that point. Give it a raised bed or mound with sharp drainage and open airflow; the Valley's summer humidity, more than its heat, is what brings on root and stem rot in a low, poorly drained spot.
new: Oregano is a hardy perennial. Texas A&M AgriLife's herb guide recommends full sun after a protected start and spacing of 8 to 10 inches; UF/IFAS gives 10 to 12 inches for air circulation. Texas A&M advises dividing perennial herbs every 3 or 4 years in early spring. Humid conditions can bring on root rot, so plant in well-drained soil with good air circulation. UF/IFAS recommends raised beds in humid central Florida to control moisture.

old: A full-size watermelon plant usually gives you 2 to 4 melons, while small icebox types make more, smaller ones. Each plant needs a lot of room. If you want bigger melons, keep just two or three fruit per vine so the plant can size them up.
new: Washington State's planning table expects about 6 to 12 melons from 3 plants in a 10-foot row. Watermelons need a lot of room. Water steadily while the fruit sets and grows. Feed them a second time after they bloom, while the fruit is growing, but don't overdo nitrogen: too much gives you more vine and less fruit.

old: Feed the vines a little as they start to run, then go easy on nitrogen, add mulch to keep the soil moist, and give them plenty of room to spread. Check under the leaves for tiny pests.
new: Plants get their first feeding before the vines start to run and a second one after they bloom, while fruit is growing. Spread mulch, such as dried grass clippings, straw, or wood chips, to save water and keep weeds down. Give the vines plenty of room to spread. Check under the leaves for aphids, which usually show up once the vines start running. In hot, dry weather, also watch for spider mites: these tiny mites leave pale yellow to reddish-brown specks on the tops of the leaves.

old: Plant the big flat fava seeds right where they will grow, about 1 to 2 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart, then thin to about 8 to 10 inches apart. Where winters are mild, plant in fall so the crop grows over winter; where winters are cold, plant as early as you can work the soil in late winter or spring. The seeds are slow to sprout, sometimes taking up to three weeks, and there is no need to start them indoors.
new: Plant the big, flat fava seeds right where they will grow, then thin the seedlings to about 8 to 10 inches apart. Favas are a cool-season crop and like highs no warmer than the low 80s °F. In Santa Clara County, California, UC Master Gardeners sow them in February or from August to September, sometimes into October, and fall-planted beans usually start producing in early spring. University of Minnesota Extension says to plant them early in spring, the way you would peas.
